title: Eccles Cakes
subtitle: flaky pastry filled with currants and spiced butter
excerpt: Eccles cakes are round pastries made from puff pastry filled with currants, brown sugar, and spiced butter. The pastry blisters and glazes in the oven to give a crisp, caramelised finish. Makes about 12.
sourceNotes: Eccles cakes are associated with the town of Eccles in Greater Manchester, where they were sold commercially from the late 18th century. Elizabeth Raffald, The Experienced English Housekeeper (1769, Project Gutenberg), gives a recipe for 'sweet patties' with currants and spiced butter enclosed in short paste that closely resembles the Eccles cake format. The defining feature is the use of puff pastry or rough puff, producing a blistered, flaky exterior. They are traditionally eaten with Lancashire cheese.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked Eccles cakes on a tray, then bag. Bake from frozen at 200°C fan for 25 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the filling a day ahead and keep refrigerated. Assemble and bake on the day.

glossaryTerms.definition: A laminated pastry made from many thin layers of butter and dough. When baked, the water in the butter turns to steam and puffs the layers apart, creating the characteristic light, flaky texture. Ready-made all-butter puff pastry works well here.
Citrus peel preserved in sugar syrup, used in British baking to add a bitter-sweet citrus flavour. A small amount in Eccles cake filling adds depth without being identifiable.

content.text: Eccles cakes make about 12 and take around 45 minutes from mixing the filling to cooling on a rack. The filling is simple: currants softened in melted butter with brown sugar, mixed spice, and a little
. The pastry does most of the work: the butter in
blisters in the oven, the egg-and-sugar glaze caramelises, and the result is a crisp, burnished shell around a soft, aromatic centre.

The key step when assembling is to seal the pastry well and then slash the top so steam can escape. Without the slashes the cakes puff wildly in one direction; with them, the pastry opens neatly into three or four ridges. Roll the filled pastry ball just enough to flatten it, not so much that you break through to the filling.

Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter in a small saucepan over a low heat. Add {{currants}} of currants, {{dark-brown-sugar}} of dark brown sugar, {{mixed-peel}} of mixed peel if using, {{mixed-spice}} of mixed spice, and {{cinnamon-ground}} of ground cinnamon. Stir together and cook for 2 minutes until the sugar dissolves. Remove from the heat and leave to cool completely.
Roll {{puff-pastry}} of puff pastry out on a lightly floured surface to about 3 mm thick. Cut out 12 circles about 12 cm in diameter, using a bowl or cutter.

Place a heaped tablespoon of filling in the centre of each circle. Gather the edges up around the filling and pinch firmly to seal, making a ball. Place seam-side down on a lined baking tray. Gently flatten each ball with your hand or a rolling pin to about 1 cm thick.

Brush each cake with beaten egg. Scatter caster sugar over the top. Use a sharp knife to make three diagonal slashes across the top of each cake, cutting just through the pastry. Refrigerate for 30 minutes.

Heat the oven to 200°C fan (220°C conventional). Bake the Eccles cakes for 15 to 20 minutes until they are deep golden brown and the pastry is crisp. Cool on the tray for 10 minutes before moving, as the caramelised sugar is very hot. Eat warm or at room temperature.

items.cause: Too much filling, or seal not tight enough
items.fix: Use a level tablespoon of filling and pinch the pastry edges really firmly. Make sure no filling is caught in the seal line.

items.cause: Oven not hot enough, or cakes taken out too early
items.fix: Eccles cakes need a properly hot oven. They should be dark golden brown, not just pale gold. Give them 3 to 5 minutes more.

items.symptom: Cakes spread flat rather than puffing
items.fix: The 30-minute chill before baking is important. Cold butter in puff pastry puffs better. If the kitchen is warm, chill for longer.

content.text: Eccles cakes have been sold in and around Manchester since at least the 1790s. They are one of the more commercially stable British pastries: the format has barely changed in over two centuries. They are traditionally paired with a piece of sharp Lancashire cheese, the sweetness of the currant filling sitting against the salty, crumbly cheese. In the north of England they appear in bakeries and market stalls throughout the year, but they are particularly associated with autumn fairs and bonfire toffee season.
